title: Flow of the zeros of polynomials under iterated differentiation: the difference of consecutive inverse branches
author: Andrei Mart\'{\i}nez-Finkelshtein, Evguenii A. Rakhmanov
work: Flow of the zeros of polynomials under iterated differentiation
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Proposition (source0.tex lines 851--863, source label lem5): for two consecutive inverse branches of the differentiated-polynomial flow on a fixed disc, the difference of the inverse branches equals minus one over n zeta plus a remainder, and there is a smaller disc and a constant, depending only on the radius parameter, such that the remainder is analytic on that disc and bounded by the constant over n squared; delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 864--976 (one adjacent proof environment of 113 lines that opens and closes inside the retained span). The proof is complete and closed inside the retained span together with its retained context. It first uses the retained bound on the inverse branches at infinity to see that the difference of the inverse branches plus one over n zeta is analytic at the origin, so that it suffices to bound the remainder on a circle; it then runs an induction over the index, writes each inverse branch in terms of the previous one plus an error term, expands the derivatives of the parametrised branch through the chain rule, and controls every derivative and reciprocal derivative by the retained two-sided Cauchy-transform bounds and the retained change-of-variables identity, showing that all the error terms are uniformly bounded, which yields the stated analyticity and the quadratic bound with a constant depending only on the radius. This proposition is the quantitative step from which the article derives the convergence of the differentiated-polynomial flow and the limiting distribution of the zeros, and its proof is a complete research-level estimate rather than a textbook exercise. H2: a research-level complex-analysis proposition whose proof combines univalence and inverse-branch control, Cauchy-transform two-sided estimates, an induction with uniform remainder bounds and contour bounds; it is well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying exercises.
